hypotheses.name: Jump Rock at Waimea Bay
supportingClues: The footage is one continuous cliff-jumping scene.
The dark, blocky volcanic rock has several jumping ledges, matching Waimea Bay’s well-known Jump Rock.
The exceptionally clear turquoise water reveals a pale sandy bottom immediately below the rock, strongly fitting Waimea Bay during calm summer conditions.
The camera faces an unobstructed ocean horizon from the seaward side of the rock.

The creator is based on Oʻahu, which provides secondary contextual support but is not visual proof. ([uhfoundation.org](https://www.uhfoundation.org/sites/default/files/2025-06/UHM2025_Summer.pdf?utm_source=openai))
contradictions: The close camera angle hides Waimea Bay’s beach and the rock’s full silhouette, preventing a definitive visual match.
Black Rock on Maui is another prominent Hawaiian lava-rock jumping site with similar water and cliff characteristics. ([kaanapalibeach.net](https://kaanapalibeach.net/cliff-jumping/))

hypotheses.name: Cline Falls and the former Cline Falls hydroelectric site
supportingClues: The approximately 20-foot segmented basalt cascade closely resembles Cline Falls on the Deschutes River.
The sagebrush, sparse juniper and layered volcanic rimrock fit Central Oregon's high-desert landscape.
The concrete-and-masonry platform and old mechanical remains are consistent with the historic hydroelectric works formerly located beside Cline Falls.
All screenshots depict one continuous river and waterfall setting.
contradictions: No readable signage, geotag or distinctive skyline directly confirms the location.
Major components of the Cline Falls powerhouse and dam were removed between 2015 and 2017, so the visible industrial remnants would need to be surviving foundations or equipment.
Steelhead Falls has a similar landscape and cascade but lacks the same documented industrial remains; White River Falls has historic power infrastructure but substantially larger waterfalls.
